'''Betty Rose Weber Holz''' (September 15, 1919 – September 3, 2005) was an American mathematician who worked for the United States Army.

== Early life and education ==
Betty Rose Weber was born in Florida, the daughter of William Wilson Weber and Rosalie I. Langford Weber. Her father was a math professor.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|date=1952-09-03|title=Miss Betty Weber, Former Resident, Wed in Columbia|pages=2|work=The Index-Journal|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/87434399/miss-betty-weber-former-resident-wed/|access-date=2021-10-20|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=1966-12-17|title=Deaths and Funerals|pages=5|work=The Index-Journal|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/87435881/deaths-and-funerals/|access-date=2021-10-20|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

Weber earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[Columbia College (South Carolina)|Columbia College]] in 1940. She completed a master's degree in mathematics at the [[University of South Carolina]] in 1949, and pursued further graduate studies at the [[University of North Carolina]] and at [[American University]].<ref name=":1">[[iarchive:armyresearchdeve3419alex/page/30/mode/1up|"DOFL Researcher Proves Women Simulate Gaming in War as Well as Men"]] ''Army Research and Development Newsmagazine'' 3(April 1962): 30. via Internet Archive</ref> As a student, she won a medal for excellence in piano performance.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Holz taught mathematics at the University of South Carolina, and was an engineer with [[Melpar]], a defense contractor. Beginning in 1954, she was an analyst for the United States Army's [[Operations Research Office]], later the Research Analysis Corporation, in [[Washington, D.C.]] In 1961 she and Edward M. Girard represented the US at the American-British-Canadian Ad Hoc Working Group on [[Wargame|War Gaming]] and Simulation when it met in London.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news|date=1961-04-04|title=Ex-Columbian Will Attend May Conference in London|pages=18|work=The Columbia Record|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/87436317/ex-columbian-will-attend-may-conference/|access-date=2021-10-20|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> In the 1960s and 1970s, she helped to develop ELIM (the Enlisted Loss Inventory Model) and COMPLIP (Computation of Manpower Programs Using Linear Programming), early computer programs for modeling military manpower and logistics.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Holz|first1=Betty W.|last2=Wroth|first2=James M.|date=1981|title=The Army's Approach to Improved Strength Forecasting|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Um6rgPETvj4C&q=Betty+W.+Holz&pg=RA1-PP4|journal=Defense Management Journal|volume=18|pages=8–13}}</ref>

Holz was a member of [[Phi Beta Kappa]], the [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]], the [[Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences|Operations Research Society of America]], and the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life ==
Weber married chemical engineer Eugene Russell Holz in 1952.<ref name=":0" /> Her husband died in 1955.<ref>{{Cite news|date=1955-02-25|title=Eugene Holz Dies in Washington|pages=23|work=The Columbia Record|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/87436066/eugene-holz-dies-in-washington/|access-date=2021-10-20|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=1955-02-26|title=Holz Funeral Set for Today|pages=11|work=The Miami Herald|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/87435747/holz-funeral-set-for-today/|access-date=2021-10-20|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She died in 2005, aged 85 years, in Maryland.
